title: Programming from Zero
blurb: Algorithms, flowcharts and Python basics — explained for someone who has never written code. Covers 18.09–26.10 lectures and the full exercise sheet.

chapters.title: Thinking in steps
chapters.lead: Algorithms, the omelette, the three building blocks
chapters.html:
CHAPTER 1

Thinking in steps

Before any code: what a computer actually is, and why a recipe is the best way to think about programming.

The omelette

Your course begins with a conversation in a kitchen. Someone says “I am hungry. Let’s make an omelette.” The other person has never made one. So the first person talks them through it:

Step 1.Prepare the ingredients on the counter: 3 eggs, sunflower oil, butter, salt, black pepper. We need a pan.
Step 2.Put the pan on the stove and turn the heat to medium.
Step 3.Put 2 spoons of sunflower oil and a spoon of butter into the pan.
Step 4.Crack the eggs into the glass bowl.
Step 5.Beat the eggs.
Step 6.Add a little salt and black pepper, and whisk a bit more.
Step 7.Pour the mixture into the pan and let it cook.
Step 8.You can serve it now.

That list is an algorithm. A program is the same thing, written for a computer. Think of the computer as a very fast helper who has never cooked anything, and who does exactly what you say and nothing more.

A computer needs details

The lecture tells a second story. You ask a helper to add numbers: “Take numbers from me, calculate the sum, show the result.” It works. 14 and 35 gives 49.

Then you ask for a division in the same way, and the helper says “problem”. Adding works in any order, but dividing does not: 21 ÷ 3 is not 3 ÷ 21. So you must be specific: “Take the dividend and the divisor. Calculate dividend / divisor.” Now 21 and 3 gives 7.

→
The big lesson
A computer never guesses what you meant. If a step could be understood in two ways, it is not good enough. This is the “definiteness” rule below.

What is an algorithm?

✓
Learn this definition word for word
An algorithm is a method of solution that is expressed as a sequence of finite steps.

Every algorithm has four characteristics:

CharacteristicWhat the slides sayIn plain words
InputAn algorithm may or may not require input.It might need ingredients from you. It might not.
OutputEach algorithm is expected to produce at least one result.There must be an omelette at the end.
DefinitenessEach instruction must be clear and unambiguous.“Add a bit of something” is not allowed.
FinitenessIf the instructions are executed, the algorithm should terminate after a finite number of steps.It must end. It cannot cook forever.

The three building blocks

Algorithms and flowcharts are built from only three control structures. Every program in this course is a mix of these:

StructureMeaningEveryday example
1. SequenceDo this, then this, then this.Crack the eggs, then beat them.
2. Branching (Selection)Choose one path based on a question.If it is raining, take an umbrella. Otherwise, take sunglasses.
3. Loop (Repetition)Repeat some steps.Keep whisking until the mixture is smooth.

chapters.title: Flowcharts
chapters.lead: The six symbols and the lecturer’s notation
chapters.html:
CHAPTER 2

Flowcharts: an algorithm as a drawing

A flowchart shows the same steps as an algorithm, using shapes and arrows. Exam questions ask you to draw them and to turn them into code.

What is a flowchart?

  • The first flowchart design goes back to 1945 and, according to the slides, was designed by John von Neumann.
  • Unlike an algorithm written in words, a flowchart uses different symbols to design a solution.
  • By looking at one, you can understand the operations and the order they happen in.
  • A flowchart is often considered a blueprint of a design used to solve a specific problem.

A free tool for drawing them is app.diagrams.net.

The six symbols

NameSymbolWhat it is forExample
OvalThe start and the end of the flowchart.Start, Stop
ParallelogramInput and output.TAKE a, SHOW result
DiamondA decision. There are alternatives, usually true and false.a > b ?
RectangleProcessing: calculations and changing data.sum ← a + b
ArrowsFlow lines. They connect the symbols and show the order.→
Predefined processA function: a group of steps doing one task, defined elsewhere.w = f(c)
★
Memory trick
Parallelogram = the computer talks with a person (TAKE, SHOW). Rectangle = the computer thinks alone. Diamond = a question with two exits.

How your lecturer writes things

Exams say “write an algorithm” and “draw the flowchart”, so copy this style:

NotationMeaning
Step 1. Step 2. …Numbered steps, in order.
Step 3.1A step that sits inside step 3, such as the “then” part of an “if”.
sum ← a + bThe left arrow means “store the result in”. Calculate the right side, then put it in sum.
if … then … else …A branch: a true part and a false part.
go to step 3Jump back. This creates a loop.
TAKE, SHOWInput and output.
i | N“i divides N” with nothing left over. 3 | 12 is true. 5 | 12 is false.
N mod 10The remainder after dividing. 851 mod 10 = 1.
small empty circleA merge point, where several arrows join into one.

Example: summing numbers

Step 1.Take numbers.
Step 2.Calculate summation.
Step 3.Show result.

Dividing looks the same, but the input is named exactly:

Step 1.Take dividend and divisor.
Step 2.Calculate division as dividend / divisor.
Step 3.Show result.
★
You can combine
Two processes can share one rectangle, as long as you write them in the correct order.
!
Order matters
“a ← b” then “b ← a” does not swap anything. By the second step, the old value of a is gone. There is more on this in Chapter 3.

chapters.title: Your first Python program
chapters.lead: Variables, types, input and print, operators
chapters.html:
CHAPTER 3

Your first Python program

Python is the language we write these steps in. This chapter covers the vocabulary: storing values, asking the user, doing maths, showing answers.

Reading a whole program first

Here is the volume of a cylindrical tank, V = π r² h. Read it like a recipe. The computer goes through the lines from top to bottom, one at a time.

LineWhat it means in EnglishAlgorithm step
1–2Ask for the radius and height, and remember them as r and h.Step 1. Take r and h
3Calculate the volume and remember it as V.Step 2. V ← π·r·r·h
4Show the answer on the screen.Step 3. Show V

Variables: labelled boxes

A variable is a box with a name on it, holding one value. The line age = 20 means “put 20 in the box called age”. If you put in something new, the old value is thrown away.

!
= does not mean “equals” here
x = x + 1 looks impossible in maths. In Python, = means “store”. It works out the right side using the old x, then stores the answer back in x. Your lecturer’s arrow says it better: x ← x + 1. To ask whether two things are equal, use two equals signs: ==.

Naming rules

  • Must start with a letter or underscore.
  • Cannot start with a number.
  • Only letters, digits and underscores (A–z, 0–9, _).
  • Case-sensitive: age, Age and AGE are three different variables.
  • Cannot be a Python keyword, such as not.
NameOK?
my_name, _my_name✓
midterm1, midterm_1✓
e_posta_adresi✓
my-name (has a dash)✗
age!of!you (has !)✗
1st_midterm (starts with a digit)✗
not (keyword)✗
i
A small detail
The lecture notes also list print, int and input as names not to use. Strictly, Python would allow them, but you would break those tools for the rest of your program. In the exam, treat them as forbidden.

Data types: kinds of values

TypeShort forHoldsExamples
intintegerwhole numbers7, -3, 2026
floatfloating pointdecimal numbers3.14, 15.0
strstringtext, in quotes"volkan", "7"
boolbooleanonly True or FalseTrue, False
complexcomplex numbernumbers with an imaginary part1j is i in Python

The slides also list these other built-in types by name. You only need to recognise that they exist: list, tuple, range, dict, set, frozenset, bytes, bytearray, memoryview, NoneType.

Talking to the user

input("question") shows the question and waits for typing. What it gives back is always text, even if a number was typed. Text can’t be used in maths, so we convert it:

You writeYou getUse it for
input("…")textwords
int(input("…"))a whole numbercounts, integers
float(input("…"))a decimal numbermeasurements, anything with a point

print(…) shows something on the screen. There are two common ways to mix text with values:

★
Comments
Anything after # is a note for humans. The computer ignores it.

Maths in Python

SymbolMeaningExampleResult
+ -add, subtract7 - 25
*multiply3 * 412
/divide851 / 1085.1
//integer part of a division851 // 1085
%remainder (mod)851 % 101
**power2 ** 38
!
Never write r^2
The lecturer’s warning: “Do NOT use r^2!” In Python, ^ is a different operation, and it will silently give you a wrong number. For powers use r ** 2 or m.pow(r, 2).
!
Division always gives a decimal
If an expression contains / or at least one float, the result is a float. 10 / 2 is 5.0, not 5. With whole numbers, // gives a whole number, or you can wrap a result: int(25.5) gives 25. Careful with negatives: // always rounds down, so -7 // 3 is -3, while int(-7 / 3) is -2.
!
Parentheses change the answer
Python multiplies and divides before it adds, going left to right. -b + m.sqrt(delta) / (2*a) only divides the square root. (-b + m.sqrt(delta)) / 2*a divides by 2 and then multiplies by a. The correct form is (-b + m.sqrt(delta)) / (2*a).

The remainder is a superpower

QuestionPythonWhy
Is n even?n % 2 == 0Dividing by 2 leaves nothing.
Does 5 divide n?n % 5 == 0Dividing by 5 leaves nothing.
Last digit of n?n % 10851 % 10 is 1.
Remove the last digit?n // 10851 // 10 is 85.

Shortcuts

ShortcutSame asNote
i += 1i = i + 1The most common line in this course
n -= dn = n - d
f *= if = f * i
x /= 2x = x / 2
f1 = f2 = 1both become 1
s, B = N2, N1s = N2 and B = N1 at the same momentSwapping: a, b = b, a

Extra tools: import

Python keeps extra tools in packages. import math as m brings in the maths package and gives it the short nickname (alias) m. Other common ones are sympy as sp and numpy as np.

!
Order again
A value must exist before it is used. If you write pi = 3.14159, it must come before the line that calculates V.

chapters.title: Making decisions
chapters.html:
CHAPTER 4

Making decisions: if, elif, else

The second building block, branching. The program asks a yes-or-no question and takes a different path depending on the answer.

True-or-false questions

A condition (also called a logical expression) is a question whose answer is True or False.

WriteMeansExample that is True
==equal?3 == 3
!=not equal?3 != 4
< >less than, greater than2 < 5
<= >=less or equal, greater or equal5 >= 5

You can join questions together:

WordTrue whenExample
andboth sides are trueN1 % i == 0 and N2 % i == 0
orat least one side is trueN == 0 or N == 1
notflips the answernot (N == 0 or N == 1) is the same as N != 0 and N != 1

The if statement

!
Colon and indentation
The line ends with a colon :. The lines that belong inside are pushed to the right. This is called indentation, and it is not just decoration. It is how Python knows which lines are inside the if. print("done") above is not indented, so it runs either way.

Worked example: roots of a quadratic

For a polynomial ax² + bx + c, the roots depend on delta (Δ = b² − 4ac). If delta is negative, the square root needs the imaginary number i. You don’t need the maths behind it. Just see how the choice works. The value of a must not be 0: without an x² term this isn’t a quadratic, and the code would divide by zero.

Step 1.Take a (coefficient of x²), b (coefficient of x), c (constant).
Step 2.delta ← b² − 4ac
Step 3.if delta ≥ 0 then
Step 3.1x1 ← (−b + √delta) / (2a), x2 ← (−b − √delta) / (2a)
else
Step 3.1x1 ← −b/(2a) + i·√(−delta)/(2a), x2 ← −b/(2a) − i·√(−delta)/(2a)
Step 4.Show x1 and x2.

More than two choices: elif

elif means “if the previous conditions were not true, then try this one”. Python checks from the top and stops at the first true one. The rest are skipped.

Worked example: the final grade

Avg = midterm × 0.3 + quiz × 0.2 + final × 0.5. Then use this table:

Avg90–10085–8980–8475–7970–7465–6960–6450–5949 and below
GradeAABABBCBCCDCDDFDFF
Point4.003.503.002.502.001.501.000.500.00
→
Why only >= is needed
When the program reaches avg >= 85, it already knows avg is below 90, or the first line would have caught it. So there is no need to write “between 85 and 89”. This only works if you check from the highest down.
i
A mismatch in the notes
The grade table says FD is 50–59, but the code in the notes has elif avg >= 55 for FD. We use 50 here because it matches the table. If this comes up in the exam, follow the table in the question.
★
The last possibility
The final choice needs no question. If nothing above was true, else catches everything left over. The flowchart shows this too: the last box, FF, has no diamond.

chapters.title: Repeating things
chapters.html:
CHAPTER 5

Repeating things: loops

The third building block. Loops are where most exam points are, so take this chapter slowly.

Why we need loops

To add 100 numbers, we could write 100 “take a number” steps. The lecturer’s better idea: keep a running total, like a shopping receipt.

Number typed—1310
sum (running total)01414
Step 1.Take N (how many numbers).
Step 2.sum ← 0, c ← 0 (c is a counter)
Step 3.Take a number n.
Step 4.sum ← sum + n
Step 5.c ← c + 1
Step 6.if c < N then go to step 3
Step 7.Show sum.
→
The two loop patterns

Counter: starts at 0, goes up by 1 each round. It answers “how many?”.

Accumulator: starts at 0 and adds a value each round. It answers “what is the total?”.

For a running product, like a factorial, start at 1, because anything times 0 is 0.

The for loop

for takes the items of a group one at a time. Each round is called an iteration.

PartMeaning
tA variable that holds the current item. You choose the name.
"volkan"The iterable object: anything that can be gone through item by item. A string gives one letter at a time.
Indented linesThe scope of the for. These lines repeat. The unindented print runs once, afterwards.

range(): making a list of numbers to count through

You writeGivesRule
range(6)0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5Starts at 0. 6 items, ending at 6−1.
range(2, 6)2, 3, 4, 5From start, up to but not including the end.
range(2, 22, 5)2, 7, 12, 17Third number is the step size.
range(5, 0, -1)5, 4, 3, 2, 1A negative step counts down.
range(2, S+1)2, 3, …, STo include S, end at S+1.
!
The end is never included
range(1, 5) stops at 4. This is the single most common mistake. To include N, write N + 1. To count down to 1, end at 0.
i
Why 15.0 and not 15?
Because of float(...): the numbers are decimals, so the total is a decimal too.

A loop inside a loop

The inner loop runs all its rounds for each single round of the outer loop, like a clock: the minute hand makes a full circle for each step of the hour hand. Indentation shows which line belongs to which loop.

The while loop

while repeats as long as a condition is true. Use it when you don’t know in advance how many rounds you need.

!
The infinite loop
Lecturer’s note: “be sure, after a while, condition must be FALSE.” If you forget i += 1, then i stays 1, the condition stays true, and the loop never ends. A while needs three things: prepare the counter before the loop, test it in the condition, and change it inside.

break and continue

WordWhat it doesIn the kitchen
breakLeave the loop right now.The omelette burned. Stop cooking.
continueSkip the rest of this round and start the next.This egg is bad. Throw it away and take the next one.

while True: the “loop with a check in the middle”

while True: would run forever, so inside there must be a break. This is the easy way to turn a flowchart into code when its diamond is at the bottom or the middle.

forwhile
Use whenyou know how many rounds, or have a group to go throughyou repeat until something happens
Counterhandled for youyou prepare it and change it yourself
Exampleadd N numbers; factorialEuclid’s GCD; sum of digits

chapters.title: Functions
chapters.html:
CHAPTER 6

Functions: a recipe you can reuse

When a task appears several times, give it a name once, then just call it by name.

The idea

The slides say: a function is a block of code which only runs when it is called. A function can return data as a result. A function helps to avoid code repetition. Another word for it is a method.

Think of a “Make Tea” card. Writing the card doesn’t make any tea. Nothing happens until someone says “make tea”. Then they follow the card and hand you a cup.

PartMeaningTea card
def“I am defining a function.”Writing the card
factorialThe name you choose.“Make Tea”
(n)Parameters: the values it needs to calculate the result.“how many cups?”
indented linesThe scope of the function: its steps.The steps on the card
return fHand the result back to whoever asked.Handing you the cup

The computer skips over lines 1–5 at first, since they are only the definition. It starts on line 8. On line 9 we call factorial(n). It jumps up with the given number, calculates, and return brings the result back to where the call was.

Why it helps: the binomial coefficient

The formula C(n, r) = n! / ((n−r)! · r!) needs a factorial 3 times. Without a function we would write the same loop three times.

★
Functions can call functions
c calls factorial. The parameter names (u, v) do not need to match the names used at the call (n, r). Values are passed by position: n goes to u, r goes to v.
★
In a flowchart
A function call is drawn with the double-sided box, like w = f(c).

Worked example: a long sum

Calculate 1 + x/1! + x²/2! + x³/3! + … + xM/M!, with M = 50 and x given by the user. This combines two older ideas: summing with a loop (02.10) and factorial as a function (23.10).

Stopping when terms are too small to matter

Instead of a fixed 50 terms, we can stop as soon as a term is tinier than a chosen limit (eps, 10−15). Later terms are even smaller, so we don’t need them. We don’t know the number of rounds in advance, so we use while.

chapters.title: The classic algorithms
chapters.lead: GCD, Euclid, Fibonacci, factorial, digits, binary
chapters.html:
CHAPTER 7

The classic algorithms

Every algorithm taught in the lectures, in the order they were taught: first the idea by hand, then the steps, then the Python.

1. Greatest common divisor (GCD), trying every number

The GCD of two numbers is the biggest number that divides both. GCD of 12 and 18 is 6. The simple idea: try 2, 3, 4… up to the smaller number, and remember the last one that worked.

Step 1.Take N1 and N2.
Step 2.if N1 < N2 then
Step 2.1S ← N1
else
Step 2.1S ← N2
Step 3.gcd ← 1, i ← 2
Step 4.if i | N1 and i | N2 then
Step 4.1gcd ← i
Step 5.i ← i + 1
Step 6.if i ≤ S then go to step 4
Step 7.Show gcd.
★
Why gcd starts at 1
1 divides everything. If no other number works, the answer is 1.

2. GCD, faster: count down and stop

If we start from the top, the first match is the biggest. So we can stop right there with break. Starting at S and going down to 1 needs range(S, 0, -1).

3. GCD, the clever way: Euclid’s algorithm

Divide the big number by the small one. Then the small one becomes the new big one, and the remainder becomes the new small one. Repeat until the remainder is 0. The last divisor is the GCD.

120 and 50781 and 4841071 and 462
120 = 50·2 + 20
50 = 20·2 + 10
20 = 10·2 + 0
GCD = 10		781 = 484·1 + 297
484 = 297·1 + 187
297 = 187·1 + 110
187 = 110·1 + 77
110 = 77·1 + 33
77 = 33·2 + 11
33 = 11·3 + 0
GCD = 11		1071 = 462·2 + 147
462 = 147·3 + 21
147 = 21·7 + 0
GCD = 21
Step 1.Take N1 and N2.
Step 2.if N1 < N2 then
Step 2.1S ← N1, B ← N2
else
Step 2.1S ← N2, B ← N1
Step 3.r ← B mod S
Step 4.B ← S, S ← r
Step 5.if r ≠ 0 then go to step 3
Step 6.Show B.

4. Fibonacci numbers

Start with 1, 1. Each new number is the sum of the two before it: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, … The 7th is 13.

Step 1.Take n.
Step 2.f1 ← 1, f2 ← 1, i ← 3
Step 3.fN ← f1 + f2
Step 4.i ← i + 1
Step 5.f1 ← f2, f2 ← fN
Step 6.if i ≤ n then go to step 3
Step 7.Show fN.
!
Order is important
In step 5, f1 must take f2 before f2 changes. Reverse them and the old f2 is lost. In Python, f1, f2 = f2, fn does both at once, safely.
i
A limit of this code
For n = 1 or n = 2 the loop never runs, so fn is never created and the program crashes. The answer there should be 1. Writing fn = 1 before the loop fixes it.

5. Sum of even Fibonacci numbers below N

For N = 50: the evens are 2, 8 and 34, so the answer is 44. We don’t know how many Fibonacci numbers fit below N, so we use while True with a break.

i
Small print
The question says “less than N” while the code tests fn > N. So if N itself is a Fibonacci number, it gets counted. For strict “less than”, use fn >= N.

6. Factorial

N! is the product of all the whole numbers from 2 up to N. 5! = 5·4·3·2 = 120. By definition, 0! and 1! are both 1.

Step 1.Take N.
Step 2.f ← 1, i ← 2
Step 2.5if N = 0 or N = 1 then go to step 6
Step 3.f ← f * i
Step 4.i ← i + 1
Step 5.if i ≤ N then go to step 3
Step 6.Show f.
★
Why no check for 0 and 1 in the code?
The notes first write if not (N == 0 or N == 1):, then remove it. For N = 0 or 1, i <= N is false from the start, so the loop just never runs and f stays 1. Correct, with no extra line.

7. How many digits?

7884 has 4 digits, because it is below 10⁴ but not below 10³. So compare N with 10, 100, 1000… until it is smaller.

Step 1.Take N.
Step 2.i ← 1
Step 3.if N < 10i then show i, stop.
Step 4.i ← i + 1
Step 5.go to step 3

8. Sum of the digits

For 851: % 10 peels off the last digit, // 10 removes it. Repeat until nothing is left.

Nk = N % 10s
85111
8556
8814
0stop14
Step 1.Take N.
Step 1.5s ← 0
Step 2.k ← N mod 10
Step 2.5s ← s + k
Step 3.N ← (N − k) / 10
Step 4.if N ≠ 0 then go to step 2
Step 5.Show s.
i
Positive numbers only
These digit programs assume N is not negative. With a negative number, // rounds down and gets stuck at −1, so while N != 0 would never end. To handle negatives, start with N = abs(N).
!
/ versus //
In the notes, N = (N - k) / 10 printed 17.0 instead of 17, because / always makes a float. N // 10 keeps it a whole number. int((N - k) / 10) also works.

9. A decimal fraction in binary

Computers count in base 2, using only 0 and 1. To convert a number between 0 and 1, such as 0.8125: double it. If the result is 1 or more, the next binary digit is 1, and you remove that 1. If not, the digit is 0. Repeat until nothing is left.

N2 × NDigitN − digit
0.81251.62510.625
0.6251.2510.25
0.250.500.5
0.51.010

Reading the digits from top to bottom: 0.8125 in base 10 is 0.1101 in base 2.

Step 1.Take N.
Step 2.N ← 2N
Step 3.if N ≥ 1 then
Step 3.5digit ← 1
else
Step 3.5digit ← 0
Step 4.Show digit.
Step 5.N ← N − digit
Step 6.if N ≠ 0 then go to step 2

10. Reject negatives, stop at zero

This is the program at the end of Chapter 5 (lecture of 23.10). In its flowchart, the arrow back from number < 0 acts as continue, and the arrow out at number = 0 acts as break. The main loop itself has no condition, which is why it becomes while True:.

The question in the lecture also says to count how many numbers are positive, although the lecture’s solution only shows the sum. Here is the full version, with the count added:

chapters.title: Exam question types
chapters.lead: A method for each, plus a final checklist
chapters.html:
CHAPTER 8

How to answer each exam question type

The exercise sheet has five kinds of question. Here is a method for each.

Type A: “Write all values” (tracing)

Pretend to be the computer. Draw one column per variable and go line by line. Each time a value is assigned, write it down. Do not skip lines, and do not use your intuition.

Line reacheditWhat happened
10t starts at 0
21range gives 1
310 + 1
22range gives 2
331 + 2
23range gives 3
363 + 3. Done: 4 is not included
!
range is not affected by the body
If you change i inside a for, the next round still takes the next number from range, as if nothing happened. This is the trick in exercise 2.

Type B: Flowchart → Python

In the flowchartIn Python
Oval (Start, Stop)Nothing. It’s just the beginning and the end of the file.
Parallelogram TAKE xx = int(input("…"))
Parallelogram SHOW xprint(x)
Rectangle x ← y + 1x = y + 1
x mod 2x % 2
i | A (i divides A)A % i == 0
Diamond with no arrow going backif … else …
Diamond at the top of a loopwhile condition:
Diamond at the bottom or middle of a loopwhile True: and if …: break
Double-sided box w = f(c)def f(x): … at the top, and w = f(c) here
★
Check which way the arrow leaves
Python’s while continues on true. If the flowchart leaves the loop on True, like “x ≥ y → SHOW”, then flip the question: while not x >= y:, or simply while x < y:.

Type C: Problem → algorithm → flowchart → code

  1. Try it by hand with small numbers. How did you do it?
  2. Name the boxes you needed (a total, a counter).
  3. Write the steps in the Step 1, Step 2 style.
  4. Draw the flowchart: one shape per step, and an arrow back for every “go to”.
  5. Write the code, then test with your hand example.
If the question saysThink of
“sum of…”, “total”accumulator: s = 0, s += x
“how many…”, “count”counter: c = 0, c += 1
“average”both: total ÷ count. Check the count isn’t 0
“divisible by”, “even”, “odd”%
“100 numbers”, “N numbers”for i in range(N):
“until…”, “when zero is entered”while True: and break
different results for different rangesif / elif / else
“digits of a number”% 10 and // 10

Type D: for → while

A for i in range(a, b, c): is the same as these three pieces. Move them to the right places.

!
Nested loops
The inner counter must be reset inside the outer loop, so it restarts every time.
!
Two cases where the pattern needs care

If the body uses continue: continue would jump over i += c and the loop might never end. Do the i += c before the continue too.

If the body changes i: a for ignores that change, as exercise 2 showed, but a while does not. Count with a separate variable, so the body’s changes to i can’t affect the counting.

Type E: Fill in the blanks

Work out what the finished program should do, write down the list of values you need, then choose the range. Test the first and last value. “2 to 12, even” becomes range(2, 13, 2).

Before you hand in: a checklist

  • Every if, elif, else, for, while and def line ends with :.
  • Lines inside are indented. Lines after are not.
  • == when asking, = when storing.
  • ** for powers, never ^.
  • Every input that needs a number is wrapped in int(…) or float(…).
  • Totals and counters are set up before the loop, not inside it.
  • Every while changes something, so it can end.
  • Division has brackets around the whole top and the whole bottom.
  • In flowcharts: oval, parallelogram, rectangle, diamond are used correctly, and each diamond has two labelled exits.

The exercise sheet, fully solved

Try each one yourself first and cover the answer. Every program here has been run, and the output shown is real.

EXERCISE 1Write a Python program for the flowchart.

What it is: a GCD. It keeps subtracting the smaller number from the bigger one. When a reaches 0, b is the GCD. The decision is in the middle of the loop, so while True and break fit best.

chapters.title: Cheat sheet
chapters.lead: The whole course on two pages.
chapters.html:
Key definitions

  • Algorithm: a method of solution expressed as a sequence of finite steps.
  • Its 4 characteristics: input, output, definiteness, finiteness.
  • 3 control structures: sequence, branching (selection), loop (repetition).
  • Flowchart: a blueprint of a solution using symbols. First design: 1945, John von Neumann.
  • Function: a block of code that only runs when called.

Flowchart symbols

Ovalstart and end
Parallelograminput and output (TAKE, SHOW)
Rectangleprocessing (x ← y + 1)
Diamonddecision (true or false)
Arrowflow of logic
Double-sided boxpredefined process, function

Operators

/divide, always a float: 10/2 is 5.0
//integer part: 851//10 is 85
%remainder: 851%10 is 1
**power: 2**3 is 8. Never ^
== !=equal, not equal
< > <= >=comparisons
and or notboth, at least one, flip
+= -= *= /=x += 1 means x = x + 1
a, b = b, aswap

Types and conversion

int 7    float 3.14    str "hi"    bool True
int(25.5) → 25    float("3") → 3.0
n = int(input("how many? "))
x = float(input("value? "))

Printing

print("sum:", s)        # comma adds a space
print(f"sum: {s}")      # f-string
print("a\tb")           # \t tab, \n new line
print(x, end="")        # stay on the same line

Math package

import math as m
m.pi   m.sqrt(x)   m.pow(a, b)   m.cos(x)
abs(-3) → 3     1j → the complex i

Branching

if avg >= 90:
    grade = "AA"
elif avg >= 85:        # first true one wins
    grade = "BA"
else:                  # everything left
    grade = "FF"

range

range(6)0 1 2 3 4 5
range(2, 6)2 3 4 5
range(2, 22, 5)2 7 12 17
range(5, 0, -1)5 4 3 2 1
range(2, S + 1)2 3 … S (end is excluded)

Loops

for i in range(N):      # N rounds
    ...

i = 1                   # 1 prepare
while i <= 10:          # 2 test
    ...
    i += 1              # 3 change, or it never ends

while True:             # check in the middle
    ...
    if done:
        break           # leave the loop

continue                # skip to the next round

Standard patterns

s = 0                   # total
c = 0                   # count
f = 1                   # product (starts at 1!)
for ... :
    s += x
    c += 1
    f *= x
if c != 0:
    print(s / c)        # average

n % 2 == 0              # n is even
n % 5 == 0              # 5 divides n
n % 10                  # last digit
n // 10                 # remove last digit
if a < b: S = a         # smaller of two

Functions

def factorial(n):       # define
    f = 1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        f *= i
    return f            # send result back

print(factorial(5))     # call → 120

The classics, in one line each

GCD simplefor i in 2..S: if i divides both, gcd = i
GCD downrange(S, 0, -1), first match, break
Euclidr = B % s; B, s = s, r until r is 0; answer B
Fibonaccifn = f1 + f2; f1, f2 = f2, fn
Factorialf = 1; f *= i for i in 2..N
Digit countsmallest i with N < 10**i
Digit sums += N % 10; N = N // 10 until 0
Fraction to binarydouble; digit is 1 if ≥ 1; subtract digit
Seriessumm += x**k / factorial(k)

Flowchart to Python

TAKE xx = int(input())
SHOW xprint(x)
x mod 2x % 2
i | AA % i == 0
Diamond, no return arrowif / else
Diamond on top of loopwhile cond:
Diamond at bottom or middlewhile True + break

Top exam mistakes

  • Writing ^ instead of **
  • = where == is needed
  • Missing : or wrong indentation
  • Forgetting that range excludes the end
  • Forgetting i += 1 in a while
  • Forgetting int(...) around input
  • Bad brackets: use (-b + r) / (2 * a)
  • Wrong update order: f1 before f2
  • Setting the total to 0 inside the loop
  • Changing i in a for and expecting it to matter

quiz.q: What is an algorithm?
o: A method of solution expressed as a sequence of finite steps
quiz.why: This is the slide’s definition, word for word.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four characteristics of an algorithm?
quiz.why: The four are input, output, definiteness and finiteness.

quiz.q: “Each instruction must be clear and unambiguous.” Which characteristic is this?
quiz.why: Definite means there is only one way to understand each step.

quiz.q: What are the three control structures?
quiz.why: Sequence, branching (selection) and loop (repetition).

quiz.q: Which symbol is used for TAKE and SHOW?
quiz.why: Parallelograms mean input and output.

quiz.q: Which symbol is used for a decision?
quiz.why: A diamond has a question and at least two exits.

quiz.q: What does a rectangle with an extra line on each side represent?
quiz.why: It represents a group of steps defined elsewhere, like w = f(c).

quiz.q: According to the slides, who designed the first flowchart, and when?
quiz.why: The slides give John von Neumann, 1945.

quiz.q: Which is a valid variable name?
quiz.why: 1st starts with a digit, my-name has a dash, not is a keyword.

quiz.q: Are age and Age the same variable?
quiz.why: Capital letters matter in names.

quiz.q: What type does input() give back?
quiz.why: Always text, which is why we wrap it in int() or float().

quiz.q: How do you write r squared in Python?
quiz.why: ^ is a different operation. The lecturer warns against it.

quiz.q: What does print(7 % 3) show?
quiz.why: % gives the remainder: 7 = 3·2 + 1.

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: // keeps only the integer part.

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: / always gives a float.

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: Multiplication goes first: 3·4 = 12, then 2 + 12.

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: Both assignments happen at once, so this swaps them.

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: After a = b, the 5 is gone. Then b = a keeps 9. Order matters!

quiz.q: What is shown?
Which line asks whether x equals 3?
quiz.why: Two equals signs ask. One equals sign stores.

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: 7 % 2 is 1, so the condition is false.

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: Python stops at the first true condition. Check from highest to lowest!

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: and needs both sides. or needs only one.

quiz.q: What is the same as not (N == 0 or N == 1)?
quiz.why: The slides point this out. “Not (A or B)” means “not A and not B”.

quiz.q: Which numbers does range(4) give?
quiz.why: It starts at 0, with 4 items, and doesn’t include 4.

quiz.q: Which numbers does range(2, 22, 5) give?
quiz.why: Start at 2, add 5, stop before 22.

quiz.q: Which range gives 5, 4, 3, 2, 1?
quiz.why: The end is not included, so stop at 0.

quiz.q: Which range gives 2, 3, …, S?
quiz.why: To include S, end at S + 1.

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: A string gives one letter each round. end="" keeps them on one line.

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. The 4 isn’t included.

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: continue skips only round 2.

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: break leaves the whole loop.

quiz.q: What is wrong with this code?
o: It never ends, because i never changes
quiz.why: This is an infinite loop. i += 1 is missing.

quiz.q: What is shown?
quiz.why: 10 → 5 → 2 → 1, then the condition is false.

quiz.q: What is the starting value of a running product, like factorial?
quiz.why: Anything times 0 stays 0.

quiz.q: Which keyword creates a function?
quiz.why: def means define.

quiz.q: When does the code inside a function run?
o: At the end of the program
As soon as Python reads it
quiz.why: Slide: “a block of code which only runs when it is called”.

quiz.q: What is shown?
What does return do?
o: Sends a result back to where the function was called
quiz.why: It hands back the result. print only shows it.

quiz.q: Using Euclid’s algorithm, what is the GCD of 120 and 50?
What is the 7th Fibonacci number?
What is shown?
What is 0.8125 in binary?
quiz.why: Doubling gives digits 1, 1, 0, 1.

quiz.q: Why can GCD with a countdown use break?
o: The first match when counting down is the biggest
quiz.why: Once we find a match from the top, nothing later can beat it.

cards.back: A method of solution expressed as a sequence of finite steps.
Input, output, definiteness, finiteness.
Sequence, branching (selection), loop (repetition).
A blueprint of a solution using symbols. First design 1945, John von Neumann (per the slides).
Start and end of a flowchart.
Input and output: TAKE, SHOW.
Processing: calculations, x ← y + 1.
A decision, with True and False exits.
Predefined process, a function: w = f(c).
A named box holding one value.
= stores a value. == asks whether two values are equal.
/ divides (always a float). // gives the integer part. % gives the remainder.
r ** 2 or m.pow(r, 2). Never r^2.
Text, always. Wrap it: int(input()) or float(input()).
f"sum is {s}" puts the value of s inside the text.
Pushing lines to the right. It shows Python which lines are inside an if, a loop or a function.
“If the previous conditions were not true, try this one.” The first true condition wins.
2, 7, 12, 17. Start, stop before, step.

cards.front: The three parts of a while
cards.back: Prepare the counter, test it in the condition, change it inside.
A loop whose condition never becomes false, like forgetting i += 1.
Leaves the loop immediately.
Skips the rest of this round and starts the next.
c += 1 counts how many. s += x adds up a total. Both start at 0.
1, because anything times 0 is 0.
A block of code which only runs when it is called. It can return a result and avoids repetition.
def defines a function. return sends the result back to where it was called.
A variable the function needs to calculate its result, in the brackets after its name.
n % 10 is the last digit. n // 10 removes it.
r = B % s, then B, s = s, r. Stop when r is 0. The answer is B.
fn = f1 + f2, then f1, f2 = f2, fn.
Keeps print on the same line. The default end is "\n", a new line.
How Python writes the imaginary number i.
